section_1.title: Prerequisite Recap: The Area of a Parallelogram
section_1.content: Briefly review that the absolute value of the determinant of a 2x2 matrix corresponds to the area of the parallelogram formed by its column vectors. This sets the geometric foundation for interpreting systems of linear equations.
section_1.example: Visualizing a parallelogram in a 2D plane defined by vectors v1(a, c) and v2(b, d) with area = |ad - bc|.

section_2.title: The Geometric Setup: Solving Ax = b
section_2.content: Represent a 2x2 system as a vector equation: x*v1 + y*v2 = b. Explain that we are looking for the 'weights' (x and y) that combine v1 and v2 to reach the target point b.
section_2.example: A robot arm (represented by vector b) trying to reach a coordinate by combining two base rotation vectors v1 and v2.

section_3.title: The Substitution Intuition
section_3.content: Introduce Cramer's Rule as a ratio of areas. Explain that replacing one column of the matrix with the target vector b creates a new parallelogram. The ratio of the area of this 'new' parallelogram to the 'original' area gives the scalar multiplier (x or y).
section_3.example: Demonstrating how replacing column 1 of the matrix with vector b creates a stretched parallelogram whose area is exactly x times the original area.

section_4.title: Visual Proof: Areas in Ratio
section_4.content: Show the animation of the determinant |Ax| / |A| = x. This visualizes why scaling the basis vector proportionally scales the area, effectively 'isolating' the variable.
section_4.example: A sliding animation where vector b moves along the span of v2, showing the area changes linearly with the value of x.

section_5.title: Summary and Geometric Constraint
section_5.content: Conclude by noting that if the original area (determinant) is zero, the vectors are collinear, the parallelogram collapses, and no unique solution exists. This provides a geometric intuition for why Cramer's rule fails when the determinant is zero.
section_5.example: A 'flat' parallelogram animation where the robot arm can't reach the target because v1 and v2 are trapped on the same line.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject
